newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb victims seek assurances from judge.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb victims seek assurances from judge.

text.p: Victims and relatives of those who perished in the Oklahoma City bombing sought assurances from the trial judge on Friday that he would not bar them from testifying even if they listen to the proceedings.

About 40 people expect to testify at the penalty phase of the trial if Timothy McVeigh is found guilty of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds of others.

In a request filed with the federal court, the group urged U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch to "make it clear" that he will not bar the victims from testifying during the penalty phase, when jurors will decide whether McVeigh should be executed or sentenced to life imprisonment.
The Washington-based National Organisation for Victim Assistance joined the bombing victims in the petition filed with the court.

The move was prompted by a recent ruling by Matsch in which he said he would consider barring victims from testifying at a penalty phase of the trial if he thinks their testimony was influenced by what they heard in the courtroom.

"As a result, the victim impact witnesses continue to face the excruciating choice between observing the trial and risking the exclusion of their impact testimony, or remaining eligible to testify, but not being able to observe the trial," the filing, representing 89 victims said.
"A number of the victims have been forced to give up their right to observe defendant McVeigh's trial" because of uncertainty about Matsch's decision, the victims complained.
Witnesses in federal trials normally are barred from court sessions until it is their turn to testify so what they see and hear will not influence them.
Matsch's ban extended that principle to include witnesses testifying only about how a crime has impacted their lives.

Congress last month sided with victims against Matsch on the exclusion issue. Matsch had barred, without exception, victims from attending court sessions if they would testify in a penalty phase of the trial.
Congress passed legislation overturning the ban.
